Author rationale/misconception comparison: Both sums equal c+d-a-b for any four position vectors, so both tetrahedron and unrestricted cases hold without nondegeneracy.

AB+CD=b-a+d-c. Subtracting it from p=q gives 2(c-b), which is nonzero whenever B and C differ. Some coincident cases can make B true, but it is not true for any four points. Independent counterexample: For A=(0,0,0),B=(1,0,0),C=(0,1,0),D=(0,0,1), p=q=(-1,1,1), whereas AB+CD=(1,-1,1). Author rationale/misconception comparison: AD=AB+BD gives p=AB+BD+BC; incorrectly concatenate same-tail BD+BC to CD to obtain AB+CD. Correct formula is BD-BC=CD. The standard tetrahedron counterexample exactly matches independent Phase 2.

m=(a+b)/2 and n=(c+d)/2; 2MN=2(n-m)=c+d-a-b=p=q. The directed order M->N and factor two are essential, and the formula survives coincident points. Author rationale/misconception comparison: 2[(c+d)/2-(a+b)/2]=c+d-a-b=p=q; midpoint coincidences do not invalidate it. Correct directed order M to N, factor two and null misconception.

The universal identity p=q holds in particular for all collinear points, so the asserted existence of a collinear counterexample is false. A general algebraic proof refutes the existential claim. Independent counterexample: Illustration, not the refutation's whole proof: on a line A=0,B=1,C=3,D=7, both sums are 9. Author rationale/misconception comparison: Replace signed collinear vectors with unsigned lengths at A=0,B=3,C=1,D=2: fake sums 4 and 2 produce the claimed counterexample. Actual directed sums are 2-2=0 and -1+1=0. This is a concrete wrong procedure; the universal algebra, not one example, excludes all collinear counterexamples.
